errors.name: Vague referent in a justification
non_conceptual_causes: writing habit of using pronouns for the subject of a sentence
work left unlabelled, so no name is available to refer back to
time pressure producing compressed prose

errors.scoring_consequence: The reasoning or justification point is not earned even when the stated conclusion is correct.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise modelling and requiring precise mathematical language, labelling every intermediate result so that a name is available, and describing behaviour of a function or its derivative over an interval rather than at a point.

errors.name: Linkage error equating a variable expression with a numerical value

errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise modelling the equals sign as a statement of equality rather than punctuation, never equating a variable expression with a constant, and writing notation such as the derivative evaluated at a point with an explicit subscript or argument.

errors.name: Speed decided from the sign of acceleration alone

variable of integration shares a name with a limit of integration

errors.name: Arithmetic performed with infinity and limit notation dropped

limit notation seen as an optional formality
mismatch between the limiting variable and the variable used as the upper bound

errors.name: Hypotheses of a theorem not verified before its conclusion is used
non_conceptual_causes: theorem recalled as a conclusion only
continuity assumed as obvious
the required table or graph values not quoted
errors.observed_behavior: Responses apply the Mean Value Theorem, the Intermediate Value Theorem or L'Hospital's Rule without establishing continuity from differentiability, without bounding the target value between two function values, or without confirming the indeterminate form.
errors.scoring_consequence: The condition point is not earned; in several years this was the point earned by the smallest proportion of responses on the question.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise focusing on stating and checking the hypotheses of each existence theorem, and distinguishing the Mean Value Theorem, the Intermediate Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem by their conditions.

an unnecessary rewrite undertaken when the function names would have sufficed

errors.name: Integrand chosen from the wrong area or volume family
non_conceptual_causes: formula recalled by shape of the prompt rather than by the described solid
axis of revolution read as the x-axis by default
cross section described in words not translated into an area formula

errors.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus misapplied to an accumulation function
non_conceptual_causes: lower limit of integration assumed to be zero
reversal of limits not recognised as a sign change

errors.name: Related rates differentiated with respect to the wrong variable or without the product rule
non_conceptual_causes: notation y prime used where the variable of differentiation is not stated
a relation that holds at one instant assumed to hold identically
chain rule step skipped when converting between derivatives
errors.observed_behavior: Responses differentiate an implicit relation with respect to x when time is the independent variable, omit the product rule on a product of two changing quantities, or treat one quantity as constant, and confuse the notations for the several derivatives in play.
errors.scoring_consequence: The differentiation points in the part are not earned, and the numerical answer point depends on them.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise using Leibniz notation rather than primes in related rates and implicit differentiation, emphasising the distinction between derivatives taken with respect to x and with respect to t, and providing related rates problems that arise from an implicit relation rather than a context.

errors.name: Separable differential equation separated or antidifferentiated incorrectly
non_conceptual_causes: constant factor left with the wrong differential
substitution needed for the antiderivative not performed
initial condition applied only after the algebra rather than when the constant first appears
errors.observed_behavior: Responses leave a variable on the wrong side of the separation, misplace a constant factor, produce an incorrect antiderivative of a trigonometric or reciprocal term, or mishandle the sign and the absolute value in a logarithm before solving for the dependent variable.
errors.scoring_consequence: The separation, antiderivative and constant points are assessed separately, so an early slip costs several points in the part.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise classifying worked separations as correctly separated, poorly separated or not separated, and applying the initial condition as soon as the constant of integration first appears.

errors.name: Average value confused with average rate of change
non_conceptual_causes: the two phrases treated as synonyms

division by the interval length omitted

errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise practice distinguishing the average rate of change of a function from the average value of a function, and showing that the average value of the derivative is the average rate of change of the function.

non_conceptual_causes: bound recalled as a formula without its conditions
the two bounds not distinguished by situation
inequality symbol chosen without attention to which side is the bound

fraction arithmetic done mentally
tangent line equation solved for y when point-slope form would have sufficed
errors.observed_behavior: Responses simplify a numerical or algebraic expression that the exam does not require to be simplified, and introduce sign, order of operations or fraction errors that spoil an otherwise correct result.
errors.scoring_consequence: A point already secured by the correct setup can be lost when the simplified final form is wrong.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise reminding students that the free-response section does not require simplification, while still practising the underlying arithmetic and algebra.

instances.question: Q3
instances.summary: Many responses omitted x equals 6, where the derivative graph is not differentiable, and some listed points where the derivative is zero instead.

instances.question: Q4
instances.summary: Concavity claims rested on the sign of the second derivative without tying the argument to the given graph of f prime, and some argued from the concavity of that graph.

instances.question: Q4
instances.summary: Many responses included x equals 0, omitted x equals 6, or tied the reasoning to g double prime or f prime rather than to the graph of f.

errors.name: Points of inflection misidentified or justified without the given representation
non_conceptual_causes: inflection sought where the derivative is zero
non-differentiable point on the derivative graph overlooked
second derivative invoked although only the first derivative graph is given
errors.observed_behavior: Responses omit a point where the derivative graph has a corner, include points where the derivative is zero but concavity does not change, or justify with a statement about the second derivative that is never tied to the given graph.
errors.scoring_consequence: The identification point requires the complete correct list, and the reason point requires a reason drawn from the given graph.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise requiring reasoning in graphical questions to be tied to the given graph, and practising descriptions that keep f, f prime and f double prime distinct.

instances.question: Q5
instances.summary: The most common misconception was that a slope field is a single tangent line through a point; some drew families of curves or curves with cusps.

instances.question: Q3
instances.summary: Some solution curves lay above and below the asymptote at M equals 40, or passed through the reversed point.

instances.question: Q3
instances.summary: Some responses did not extend the solution curve to t equals 4.5.

errors.name: Solution curve sketched incorrectly on a slope field
non_conceptual_causes: curve drawn freehand without following the segments
the required extent of the sketch not read from the prompt
particular solution not distinguished from the general solution
errors.observed_behavior: Sketches miss the given point, cross or sit on the horizontal asymptote implied by the equilibrium slope segments, stop short of the edge of the field, show cusps, or present a family of curves instead of the particular solution.
errors.scoring_consequence: The sketch is scored against several features, so a curve that crosses the asymptote or stops short loses the point.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise practising sketches of several kinds of solution behaviour, and using information in the stem to form a mental picture of the curve before drawing it.

instances.question: Q5
instances.summary: Many responses did not label their work, making it hard to locate errors, and many failed to distribute the subtraction.

instances.question: Q5
instances.summary: Responses added instead of subtracted, antidifferentiated a literal f prime incorrectly, or multiplied two antiderivatives together.

instances.question: Q5
instances.summary: Incorrect choices of u and dv, a wrong sign on the cosine antiderivative, missing parentheses, and an omitted constant of integration.

errors.name: Integration by parts executed or bounded incorrectly
non_conceptual_causes: tabular layout used without labels
sign of the by parts identity misremembered
limits written on only one of the two pieces
errors.observed_behavior: Responses add instead of subtract the second integral, choose u and dv the wrong way round, multiply two antiderivatives together, antidifferentiate the second factor incorrectly, or misplace the limits of integration between the uv term and the remaining integral.
errors.scoring_consequence: The technique point and the evaluation point are separate, so an unlabelled or mis-signed application loses at least one of them.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise significant practice with a clear delineation of u and dv, labels on intermediate steps including tabular work, and writing bounds on the uv term and on the remaining integral.

instances.question: Q5
instances.summary: Some responses used the wrong initial value, used a wrong derivative value in a step, or added a third step.

instances.question: Q5
instances.summary: Errors included an incorrect form for the step, an incorrect step size of 0.4, and a slope computed at the wrong x on the second step.

errors.name: Euler's method step size or initial value applied incorrectly
non_conceptual_causes: step count read but the size not computed
the wrong table entry used as the initial value
steps not laid out in a labelled table
errors.observed_behavior: Responses start from the wrong initial value, use a step size other than the one implied by the requested number of equal steps, evaluate the slope at the wrong point on the second step, or add a third step.
errors.scoring_consequence: The first step point and the answer point are separate, so a slip after a correct first step loses only the answer point.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise clear communication of the steps and labels in Euler's method, particularly when a tabular presentation is used, and error analysis activities built around organisational strategies.

instances.question: Q1
instances.summary: Many interpretations of the derivative failed to describe the value as a rate of a rate or to say that the rate was decreasing.

instances.question: Q1
instances.summary: Responses had difficulty giving a correct interpretation containing the phrases average temperature and the interval from t equals 0 to t equals 12.

instances.question: Q1
instances.summary: Some responses reported that the temperature was decreasing, which was true but did not answer what was asked.

instances.question: Q5
instances.summary: Many responses identified the integral as an arc length but made no mention of the interval, and some called it a distance.

errors.name: Interpretation of a value in context left incomplete
non_conceptual_causes: interpretation written before the units are settled
interval named in the stem not repeated in the answer
the word rate used once where a rate of a rate is meant
errors.observed_behavior: Responses interpret a derivative or an integral without naming the quantity, the interval, or the fact that a rate is itself changing, or they answer a different question than the one asked.
errors.scoring_consequence: The interpretation point requires the key phrases, so an answer missing the interval or the rate of a rate is not earned.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise using the language of the course framework as a template for interpretations, and drawing on published scoring guidelines to see the terminology that earns interpretation points.

instances.question: Q4
instances.summary: Some responses assumed each rectangle had width 3, and many made errors in simplifying the sum; some reported a positive value despite computing a negative one.

instances.question: Q1
instances.summary: A few responses provided a left Riemann sum where a right Riemann sum was asked.

instances.question: Q1
instances.summary: Setups such as a bare sum of three values, a right Riemann sum, and a common width of 3 for unequal subintervals.

instances.question: Q3
instances.summary: Some responses used a trapezoid formula built on differences of the function values rather than sums, and one copy error in the sum cost the answer point.

errors.name: Riemann or trapezoidal sum setup insufficient or malformed
non_conceptual_causes: subinterval widths read as uniform from an evenly printed table
products collapsed before being written down
trapezoid formula recalled with a subtraction
errors.observed_behavior: Responses assume a common subinterval width where the table gives unequal ones, present the sum of the values without the widths, use the wrong sum type, or apply an incorrect trapezoid area formula.
errors.scoring_consequence: The setup point requires the sum of the appropriate products to be visible; the answer point follows it.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise requiring enough work to demonstrate the sum type in use, and connecting the definite integral of a rate to the accumulated quantity in applied contexts.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: Responses inverted the slope quotient, and for total distance used a one-dimensional arc length or the Pythagorean combination of two separate integrals.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: Some responses reported the velocity vector rather than the acceleration vector, and some reversed its components.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: Speed defined as the absolute value of dy/dx, distance written as a sum of two separate integrals, and direction of motion argued from dy/dx rather than dy/dt.

errors.name: Parametric and vector motion quantity set up incorrectly
non_conceptual_causes: formula recalled from the single-variable case
components differentiated symbolically by hand rather than with the calculator
derivative with respect to the parameter confused with the derivative along the path
errors.observed_behavior: Responses invert the quotient for the slope of the path, report a velocity vector where an acceleration vector was asked or reverse its components, compute a one-dimensional arc length or a Pythagorean combination of two separate integrals for total distance, or reason from dy/dx where dy/dt determines the direction of motion.
errors.scoring_consequence: The setup point for the requested quantity is lost, and the answer point follows it.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise using the given derivative names rather than copying expressions, comparing the arc length formulas for single variable and parametric equations, and using the calculator for component derivatives.

instances.question: Q1
instances.summary: Many responses answered that the temperature was decreasing because the first derivative was negative, which was true but did not answer whether the rate of change was increasing or decreasing; the report states the correct argument uses the positive second derivative on the interval.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: Responses argued the particle was moving toward the x-axis from the sign of dy/dx or said only that y is decreasing rather than that the derivative is negative.

errors.name: Direction of change confused with the sign of the quantity itself
non_conceptual_causes: the words increasing and decreasing attached to the quantity rather than to its rate
both derivative signs available and combined without reason
the question read as asking whether the quantity itself is increasing
errors.observed_behavior: Responses answer a question about whether a quantity is changing at an increasing or decreasing rate by appealing to the sign of the first derivative, or by pointing to the opposing signs of the first and second derivatives, rather than to the sign of the second derivative alone.
errors.scoring_consequence: The reasoning point is not earned even when the stated conclusion is correct.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise precise language separating a quantity, its rate of change and the rate at which that rate changes, and requiring the reasoning to name which derivative is being used.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: Incorrect derivatives of the polar radius, and decimal presentation errors.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: Failing to square the polar radius was the most common error, and incorrect solutions of the trigonometric equation gave wrong limits of integration.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: Local or erroneous global arguments for the point farthest from the y-axis; many did not know that the rectangular coordinate is the polar radius times the cosine of the angle.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: The chain rule product was formed from the wrong derivatives, such as dx/dt or dr/dt in place of dr/dtheta.

errors.name: Polar area and polar motion setup incorrect
non_conceptual_causes: intersection angles solved for incorrectly in a trigonometric equation
the one half constant and the limits handled after the integrand rather than with it
the relation between the rectangular coordinate and the polar radius not recalled
errors.observed_behavior: Responses omit the square on the polar radius in an area integrand, choose limits of integration that do not correspond to the intersection angles, differentiate the polar radius incorrectly, or form the chain rule product for a rate with respect to time from the wrong pair of derivatives.
errors.scoring_consequence: The integrand point is lost when the square is missing, and later points in the part are typically unreachable.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise just-in-time review of polar features introduced in precalculus, and practice writing setups and justifications even on calculator active questions.

instances.question: Q1
instances.summary: Responses wrote the rate function equal to its own definite integral, placed a summation sign before the integral, or appended a constant of integration to a definite integral; some reversed the limits or used limits of 6 and 10.

instances.question: Q1
instances.summary: The report notes that most responses displayed the required definite integral correctly, so these notational statements were the minority pattern.

errors.name: Definite integral expression written in malformed notation
non_conceptual_causes: integral notation assembled from remembered fragments
indefinite and definite integral notation not separated
limits taken from the wrong pair of values in the stem
errors.observed_behavior: Responses asked for an integral expression write statements that are not integral expressions, such as the function set equal to its own integral, a summation sign placed in front of an integral, or a constant of integration attached to a definite integral, and some reverse the limits or use limits that were never given.
errors.scoring_consequence: The expression point is not earned, since the requested object is an integral expression and nothing else is being scored in that part.
errors.teacher_advice: The report advises practising notational fluency by presenting the same communicated mathematics in several equivalent representations (cr-22:4).

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: Many responses created a variable s, wrote the area as its square and differentiated, but never stated that s is the difference of the two given functions.

instances.question: Q2
instances.summary: The report states that many students introduced variables without clearly defining them, which made it difficult for them to see the connection to the given functions.

errors.name: Variable introduced without being defined
non_conceptual_causes: a general formula recalled in its own letters and used verbatim
the substitution back to the given functions left unwritten
no habit of defining a symbol where it first appears
errors.observed_behavior: Responses invent a symbol for an intermediate quantity, differentiate with it, and never state what it stands for, so the connection between the new symbol and the functions given in the stem cannot be read.
errors.scoring_consequence: The point for expressing the quantity as a function of the given variable is not earned, and the chain rule step that depends on it is unreachable.
errors.teacher_advice: The report advises modelling the definition of every variable at the point where it is first used, and using composition of functions to model a quantity as a function of time (cr-22:8).

instances.question: Q4
instances.summary: Some responses concluded that the value of the Riemann sum must be positive and reported 51 in spite of having correctly calculated negative 51.

instances.question: Q3
instances.summary: Responses carried an incorrect value from part (a) into the candidates test and did not recognise that it contradicted their own correct conclusion in part (c) that the function was decreasing on that interval.

errors.name: Reported answer contradicts the response's own work
non_conceptual_causes: expectation that a quantity of that name must be positive
final value written from memory of the expected form
no check of the answer against the work above it
errors.observed_behavior: Responses compute a correct intermediate result and then report a final value inconsistent with it, such as changing the sign of a negative sum or carrying forward an earlier incorrect value that contradicts a later correct conclusion, without noticing the conflict.
errors.scoring_consequence: The answer point is lost although the supporting work would have earned it, and in the extremum case the justification point is lost as well.
errors.teacher_advice: The report advises that when work does not lead to the stated result students should backtrack to find where the error originated rather than adjust the answer, and that every step must be consistent (cr-23:24).

instances.question: Q5
instances.summary: Several responses computed a second derivative to find the slope of the tangent line, and others held that the equation had to be solved by separation of variables first.

instances.question: Q3
instances.summary: Some responses attempted to solve the differential equation for the function in the tangent line part, which the report calls a significant misconception about a first-order differential equation.

errors.name: Differential equation solved where it already supplies the slope
non_conceptual_causes: the phrase differential equation read as an instruction to solve
the tangent line procedure recalled as requiring an explicit function
time spent on an unnecessary solution before the requested step
errors.observed_behavior: Responses asked for a tangent line or an approximation from a given differential equation first attempt to find the general solution by separation of variables, or compute a second derivative, instead of evaluating the given equation at the point.
errors.scoring_consequence: The slope point is at risk and the part is often left incomplete, since the unnecessary work consumes the part without producing the requested value.
errors.teacher_advice: The reports advise building the connection between a contextual rate and the slope of a tangent line, and reminding students that the given equation supplies the slope directly (cr-23:13).

instances.question: Q6
instances.summary: Some responses used the power rule on a position function containing a negative exponential and produced a derivative with the exponent reduced by one.

instances.question: Q6
instances.summary: The report records this alongside communication errors as the only misconceptions observed in that part, which was otherwise done well.

errors.name: Differentiation rule chosen by the shape of the expression
non_conceptual_causes: rule selected from the visual form of the expression
exponential and power functions not distinguished in the moment
derivative written in one step with no intermediate form
errors.observed_behavior: Responses apply the power rule to an exponential term, decrementing the exponent as though the variable were the base, rather than selecting the rule that matches the type of function.
errors.scoring_consequence: The derivative point is not earned, and every later part that uses the derivative inherits the error.
errors.teacher_advice: The report advises additional practice applying differentiation rules and categorising functions by the rule they require (cr-22:19).

instances.question: Q6
instances.summary: Some responses concluded from the squared variable being less than one that the variable lies between zero and one, losing the negative half of the interval.

instances.question: Q6
instances.summary: The report states that the infinity symbol is never correctly placed next to a square bracket and asks for a review of open, closed and half open interval notation.

errors.name: Absolute value dropped when an inequality is solved for an interval
non_conceptual_causes: square root of a squared quantity taken as the quantity itself
absolute value bars dropped in transcription
interval notation conventions for open, closed and unbounded ends not settled
errors.observed_behavior: Responses convert the ratio test inequality into an interval without the absolute value, producing a one sided interval, and related presentations attach the infinity symbol to a square bracket or otherwise misuse interval notation.
errors.scoring_consequence: The interval point is not earned even where the limit of the ratio was found correctly.
errors.teacher_advice: The report advises using absolute values wherever they are appropriate and never omitting them without explanation, and reviewing interval notation (cr-22:31 and cr-22:21).

instances.question: Q6
instances.summary: A very frequent error was failing to recognise the geometric series and offering the sum of the first few terms as the value.

instances.question: Q6
instances.summary: Some responses recognised the series as geometric but were unable to determine its common ratio.

errors.name: Value of a convergent series reported as a partial sum
non_conceptual_causes: the geometric form not recognised in the given series
common ratio read from the wrong pair of consecutive terms
approximation habits carried over from error bound questions
errors.observed_behavior: Responses asked for the value of a convergent series add the first few terms and present that total, or recognise the series as geometric but cannot identify the common ratio, instead of summing it in closed form.
errors.scoring_consequence: The value point is not earned, since a decimal approximation is not the requested exact value.
errors.teacher_advice: The report advises presenting series in multiple representations so that special series such as geometric and harmonic are recognised, and notes that in this course finding the value of a convergent series calls on geometric series content (cr-22:31).
